paper.title: British Astronomy and Astrophysics Olympiad 2017-2018 — Astronomy & Astrophysics Competition Paper — Monday 22nd January 2018

documentNotes.title: Instructions
documentNotes.statement:
This question paper must not be taken out of the exam room

**Time**: 3 hours plus 15 minutes reading time (no writing permitted). Approx 45 minutes per question.

**Questions**: All four questions should be attempted.

**Marks**: The questions carry similar marks.

**Solutions**: Answers and calculations are to be written on loose paper or in examination booklets. Students should ensure their name and school is clearly written on all answer sheets and pages are numbered. A standard formula booklet with standard physical constants should be supplied.

**Instructions**: To accommodate students sitting the paper at different times, please **do not discuss** any aspect of the paper on the internet until 8 am Saturday 27th January.

**Clarity**: Solutions must be written legibly, in black pen (the papers are photocopied), and working down the page. Scribble will not be marked and overall clarity is an important aspect of this exam paper.

**Eligibility**: The International Olympiad will be held during September 2018; all sixth form students are eligible to participate, even if they will be attending university from October.

**Training Dates and the International Astronomy and Astrophysics Olympiad (IOAA)**

*The team will be selected from sixth form students taking this paper* **and** *Y12 students taking the AS Challenge in March. The best students eligible to represent the UK at the IOAA will be invited to attend the* **Training Camp** *to be held in the Physics Department at the University of Oxford,* **(Monday 9th April to Thursday 12th April 2018)**. *Astronomy material will be covered; problem solving skills and observational skills (telescope and naked eye observations) will be developed. At the Training Camp a data analysis exam and a short theory paper will be sat. Five students (plus one reserve) will be selected for further training. From May there will be mentoring by email to cover some topics and problems, followed by additional training camps in the summer.*

documentNotes.title: Important Constants
documentNotes.statement:
| Constant | Symbol | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Speed of light | $c$ | $3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ |
| Earth’s rotation period | 1 day | 24 hours |
| Earth’s orbital period | 1 year | 365.25 days |
| parsec | pc | $3.09 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{m}$ |
| Astronomical Unit | au | $1.50 \times 10^{11}\ \mathrm{m}$ |
| Radius of the Earth | $R_{\oplus}$ | $6.37 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{m}$ |
| Semi-major axis of the Earth’s orbit |  | 1 au |
| Radius of the Sun | $R_{\odot}$ | $6.96 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m}$ |
| Mass of the Sun | $M_{\odot}$ | $1.99 \times 10^{30}\ \mathrm{kg}$ |
| Mass of the Earth | $M_{\oplus}$ | $5.97 \times 10^{24}\ \mathrm{kg}$ |
| Luminosity of the Sun | $L_{\odot}$ | $3.85 \times 10^{26}\ \mathrm{W}$ |
| Stephan-Boltzmann constant | $\sigma$ | $5.67 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-2}\,K^{-4}}$ |
| Gravitational constant | $G$ | $6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m^{3}\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$ |

You might find the diagram of an elliptical orbit below useful in solving some of the questions (the diagram is shown with Question 3).

**Elements of an elliptic orbit**:

| | |
|---|---|
| $a = \mathbf{OA}\ (= \mathbf{OP})$ | semi-major axis |
| $b = \mathbf{OB}\ (= \mathbf{OC})$ | semi-minor axis |
| $e = \sqrt{1 - \frac{b^2}{a^2}}$ | eccentricity |
| F | focus |
| P | periapsis (point nearest to F) |
| A | apoapsis (point furthest from F) |

**Keplers Third Law**: For an elliptical orbit, the square of the period, $T$, of orbit of an object about the focus is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis, $a$ (the average of the minimum and maximum distances from the Sun). The constant of proportionality is $4\pi^2/GM$, where $M$ is the mass of the central object and $G$ is the universal gravitational constant.

**Magnitudes**: The apparent magnitudes of two objects, $m_1$ and $m_0$, are related to their apparent brightnesses, $b_1$ and $b_0$, via the formula:

$$\frac{b_1}{b_0} = 10^{-0.4(m_1 - m_0)}$$

documentNotes.title: Note for markers
documentNotes.statement:
**BAAO 2017/18 Solutions and Marking Guidelines**

**Note for markers:**

- Answers to two or three significant figures are generally acceptable. The solution may give more in order to make the calculation clear.
- There are multiple ways to solve some of the questions; please accept all good solutions that arrive at the correct answer. If a candidate gets the final (numerical) answer then allow them all the marks for that **part** of the question (as indicated in red), so long as there are no unphysical / nonsensical steps or assumptions made.

problems.title: Stellar Mass Loss
problems.statement: All stars lose mass during their lifetimes due to two main routes: particles escaping their surface (referred to as the stellar wind), and the mass defect of the nuclear reactions occurring in their cores.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The nebula NGC 2359 around the Wolf-Rayet star WR7. The nebula is known as Thor’s Helmet due to its resemblance to the helmet worn by the character from the Marvel Comics series. Credit: Star Shadows Remote Observatory and PROMPT/UNC.
figures.alt: Colour photograph of the nebula NGC 2359 (Thor’s Helmet): a pale blue bubble-shaped shell in the centre with red-pink filaments extending up to the left and right like the wings of a helmet, on a background of many stars.

parts.label: a. (i)
parts.statement:
a. Given that, at the distance of the Earth, the proton flux from the Sun’s stellar wind (which is assumed to be radiated equally in all directions) is $3.0 \times 10^{12}\ \mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, and that the luminosity of the Sun is solely due to the fusion of hydrogen to helium:

(i) Show that the rate at which the Sun is losing mass, $\dot{M} \equiv \frac{\mathrm{d}M}{\mathrm{d}t}$, due to its stellar wind is $\sim 10^{-14}\,M_{\odot}\ \mathrm{yr^{-1}}$. [Take the mass of a proton to be $1.67 \times 10^{-27}$ kg.]

parts.label: a. (ii)
parts.statement: Show that $\dot{M}$ due to nuclear fusion is greater than that from the solar wind.

parts.label: a. (iii)
parts.statement: Estimate how much the Earth-Sun distance and the Earth’s orbital period will have changed after the Sun has lost mass (via both routes) for one year. Assume the orbit remains circular throughout and ignore gravitational effects from all other bodies.
parts.statementAfter: In practice, the mass loss rate can vary quite considerably during a star’s lifetime, particularly once it has left the main sequence when the stellar wind can become much more substantial. Wolf-Rayet stars are massive stars near the end of their lives, presumed to be the in the stage just before a supernova, and are losing substantial amounts of mass due to very fast stellar winds. This deposits considerable energy into the surrounding interstellar medium (ISM) and can sweep up material into a thin bubble around the star, visible as a type of planetary nebula.

parts.label: b. (i)
parts.statement:
b. If every photon leaving a star is able to transfer all of its momentum (given by $p_{\mathrm{photon}} = \frac{E_{\mathrm{photon}}}{c}$) to drive a stellar wind (known as the single scattering limit):

(i) Show that the maximum mass loss rate for a star can be written in terms of the luminosity of the star, $L$, the (terminal) velocity of the stellar wind far from the star, $v_{\infty}$, and the speed of light, $c$, as

$$\dot{M}_{\mathrm{max}} = \frac{L}{v_{\infty} c}.$$

parts.label: b. (ii)
parts.statement: Hence, derive an expression for the maximum kinetic energy deposited per second by the stellar wind as a function of the luminosity of the star. Comment on your answer.

parts.label: c. (i)
parts.statement:
c. The Wolf-Rayet star WR7 is in the constellation of Canis Major and its strong winds are responsible for the nebula known as Thor’s Helmet (see Figure 1). The star has a mass of $16\,M_{\odot}$, a radius of $1.41\,R_{\odot}$, and a surface temperature of $112\,000$ K, with a measured $v_{\infty}$ of $1545\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$.

(i) Predict the mass loss rate of WR7 based upon the properties of the star, assuming the single scattering limit. Give your answer in units of $M_{\odot}\ \mathrm{yr^{-1}}$.

parts.label: c. (ii)
parts.statement: The nebula is 5 arcmins in diameter ($1^{\circ} = 60$ arcmin) and 4.8 kpc away, and at its edge is a bright thin shell of swept up material expanding at a rate of $30\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. The age of such a nebula, $t$, is related to the current values of radius, $R$, and expansion speed, $v$, by $t = 0.55R/v$. Using this model, determine the age of the nebula.

parts.label: c. (iii)
parts.statement:
If the expansion is purely driven by the direct impact of the stellar winds, then the radius at time $t$, $R(t)$, can be related to $\dot{M}$ with the formula

$$R(t) = \left(\frac{3\dot{M} v_{\infty} t^2}{2\pi n_0 m_{\mathrm{H}}}\right)^{1/4}$$

where $n_0$ is the ambient hydrogen number density in the nebula. If $n_0 = 16\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$ and $m_{\mathrm{H}} = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}$ kg, calculate the observed mass loss rate based upon the properties of the nebula. Compare it with the predicted one from earlier and comment on your answer.

answer.note: 1.25 × 10^18 kg s^-1; about 5.4 times larger than the single-scattering prediction.

parts.label: c. (iv)
parts.statement: Using your new value for $\dot{M}$, calculate the total mass expelled from the star and hence the total kinetic energy the stellar wind has so far deposited into the ISM during this stage of the star’s life.

solution.statement:
**Q1 - Stellar Mass Loss** **[Total = 25]**

**a. (i)**

$\dot{M}_{\mathrm{wind}} =$ mass flux $\times$ surface area of sphere 1 au in radius

$= (3.0 \times 10^{12} \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27}) \times (4\pi \times (1.50 \times 10^{11})^2)$ [1]

$= 1.42 \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$

$= 2.24 \times 10^{-14}\ M_{\odot}\ \mathrm{yr^{-1}}$ (so $\sim 10^{-14}\ M_{\odot}\ \mathrm{yr^{-1}}$) [1] **[2]**

**a. (ii)**

$L = \dot{M}_{\mathrm{fusion}} c^2 \quad \therefore \quad \dot{M}_{\mathrm{fusion}} = L_{\odot}/c^2 = \frac{3.85 \times 10^{26}}{(3.00 \times 10^{8})^2}$ [1]

$= 4.28 \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$ [1] **[2]**

$(= 6.78 \times 10^{-14}\ M_{\odot}\ \mathrm{yr^{-1}})$ [$so > \dot{M}_{\mathrm{wind}}$]

**a. (iii)**

$\dot{M}_{\mathrm{tot}} = \dot{M}_{\mathrm{wind}} + \dot{M}_{\mathrm{fusion}} = 9.02 \times 10^{-14}\ M_{\odot}\ \mathrm{yr^{-1}}$ [1]

In solar units, Kepler's 3rd Law is $M = a^3 / T^2$, and since the change is mass is very small compared with $M_{\odot}$ we can make the approximation $\frac{\Delta a}{a} = \frac{\Delta T}{T} = \frac{\Delta M}{M}$ [2]

So: $\Delta a = \frac{\Delta M}{M_{\odot}} a = 9.02 \times 10^{-14} \times 1.50 \times 10^{11} = 1.35 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m}$ [1]

$\Delta T = \frac{\Delta M}{M_{\odot}} T = 9.02 \times 10^{-14} \times (365.25 \times 24 \times 3600)$

$= 2.85 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{s}$ [1] **[5]**

[Allow angular momentum conservation arguments too, as well as ΔT being 3 times larger]

**b. (i)**

$p_{\mathrm{max}} = m v_{\infty} \quad \therefore \quad \frac{p_{\mathrm{max}}}{t} = \dot{M}_{\mathrm{max}} v_{\infty}$ [1]

In the single scattering limit: $p_{\mathrm{max}} = p_{\mathrm{photon}} = \frac{E}{c} \quad \therefore \frac{E}{ct} = \dot{M}_{\mathrm{max}} v_{\infty}$ [1]

(since L = E/t) $\quad \therefore \frac{L}{c} = \dot{M}_{\mathrm{max}} v_{\infty}$ [1] **[3]**

$\left(\therefore \dot{M}_{\mathrm{max}} = \frac{L}{v_{\infty} c}\right)$

**b. (ii)**

$\dot{E}_{\mathrm{K,max}} = \frac{1}{2} \dot{M}_{max} v_{\infty}^2 = \frac{1}{2} \frac{L}{v_{\infty} c} v_{\infty}^2 = \frac{1}{2} \frac{v_{\infty}}{c} L$ [1] **[1]**

Since $v_{\infty} \ll c$, this is $\ll L$ (so photons carry away much more energy) [1] **[1]**

[Also allow that as $v_{\infty} \to c$, $E_{\mathrm{K,max}} \to$ ½L]

**c. (i)**

$L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4$

$= 4\pi \times (1.41 \times 6.96 \times 10^{8})^2 \times 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \times (112000)^4$ [1]

$= 1.08 \times 10^{32}\ \mathrm{W} \quad (= 2.80 \times 10^{5}\ L_{\odot})$ [1]

$\dot{M}_{\mathrm{max}} = \frac{L}{v_{\infty} c} = \frac{1.08 \times 10^{32}}{1545 \times 10^{3} \times 3.00 \times 10^{8}} = 2.33 \times 10^{17}\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$

$= 3.69 \times 10^{-6}\ M_{\odot}\ \mathrm{yr^{-1}}$ [1] **[3]**

[Award 2 max if they forget to convert the velocity into m s$^{-1}$]

**c. (ii)**

Radius = (2.5 arcmin in radians) × (distance in metres) (we're given the diameter)

$= \left(\frac{2.5}{60} \times \frac{\pi}{180}\right) \times (4.8 \times 10^{3} \times 3.09 \times 10^{16})$ [1]

$= 1.08 \times 10^{17}\ \mathrm{m} \quad (= 3.49\ \mathrm{pc})$ [1]

$t = \frac{0.55R}{v} = \frac{0.55 \times 1.08 \times 10^{17}}{30 \times 10^{3}} = 1.98 \times 10^{12}\ \mathrm{s} \quad (\approx 63000\ \mathrm{years})$ [1] **[3]**

[Award 2 max if they forget to convert the velocity into m s$^{-1}$]

**c. (iii)**

$R(t) = \left(\frac{3\dot{M} v_{\infty} t^2}{2\pi n_0 m_{\mathrm{H}}}\right)^{\frac{1}{4}} \therefore \dot{M} = \frac{2\pi n_0 m_{\mathrm{H}} R(t)^4}{3 v_{\infty} t^2}$

$= \frac{2\pi \times 16 \times 10^{6} \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \times (1.08 \times 10^{17})^4}{3 \times 1545 \times 10^{3} \times (1.98 \times 10^{12})^2}$ [1]

$= 1.25 \times 10^{18}\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}} \quad (= 1.99 \times 10^{-5}\ M_{\odot}\ \mathrm{yr^{-1}})$ [1] **[2]**

This is (about 5.4 times) larger than the previously predicted value, suggesting the single scattering limit is not a good approximation in this situation [1] **[1]**

[In practice, multiple scattering occurs due to the Doppler Effect in the winds]

**c. (iv)**

Total mass, $M_{\mathrm{tot}} = \dot{M} t = 1.25 \times 10^{18} \times 1.98 \times 10^{12}$

$= 2.48 \times 10^{30}\ \mathrm{kg} \quad (= 1.25\ M_{\odot})$ [1] **[1]**

Total $E_{\mathrm{K,tot}} = \frac{1}{2} M_{\mathrm{tot}} v_{\infty}^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 2.48 \times 10^{30} \times (1545 \times 10^{3})^2$

$= 2.96 \times 10^{42}\ \mathrm{J}$ [1] **[1]**

[This means Wolf Rayet stars are depositing a very large amount of kinetic energy into the ISM in only a few tens of thousands of years (in this case about 2.5% of the total energy the Sun will radiate in its lifetime!)]

problems.title: Multi-Messenger Astronomy
problems.statement: GW170817 was the first gravitational wave event arising from a binary neutron star merger to have been detected by the LIGO & Virgo experiments, and careful localization of the source meant that the electromagnetic counterpart was quickly found in galaxy NGC 4993 (see Figure 2). Such a combination of two completely separate branches of astronomical observation begins a new era of ‘multi-messenger astronomy’. Since the gravitational waves allow an independent measurement of the distance to the host galaxy and the light allows an independent measurement of the recessional speed, this observation allows us to determine a new, independent value of the Hubble constant $H_0$.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Left: The GW170817 signal as measured by the LIGO and Virgo gravitational wave detectors, taken from Abbott et al. (2017). The normalized amplitude (or strain) is in units of $10^{-21}$. The signal is not visible in the Virgo data due to the direction of the source with respect to the detector’s antenna pattern. Right: The optical counterpart of GW170817 in host galaxy NGC 4993, taken from Hjorth et al. (2017).
figures.alt: Left: three stacked time-frequency spectrograms labelled LIGO-Hanford, LIGO-Livingston and Virgo, frequency axis “Frequency (Hz)” with ticks 50, 100, 500, time axis “Time (seconds)” from -30 to 0, colour bar “Normalized amplitude” 0 to 6; a rising chirp track is visible in the two LIGO panels. Right: optical image of the elliptical galaxy NGC 4993 with a small square marking the transient and an enlarged inset labelled “Aug 22”.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: The galaxy NGC 4993 is measured to have a redshift of $z = 0.00980 \pm 0.00079$. Assuming it follows Hubble’s Law, $v = H_0 d$, where $H_0 = 73.24 \pm 1.74$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, as determined by Hubble Space Telescope (HST) measurements of Cepheid variables, calculate the distance to the galaxy (in Mpc) and its (absolute) uncertainty. Give your distance to an appropriate number of significant figures.
parts.statementAfter:
Another way of measuring distances to galaxies is to use the Fundamental Plane (FP) relation, which relies on the assumption there is a fairly tight relation between radius, surface brightness, and velocity dispersion for bulge-dominated galaxies, and is widely used for galaxies like NGC 4993. It can be described by the relation

$$\log\left(\frac{D}{(1+z)^2}\right) = -\log R_e + \alpha \log \sigma - \beta \log \langle I_r \rangle_e + \gamma$$

where $D$ is the distance in Mpc, $R_e$ is the effective radius measured in arcseconds, $\sigma$ is the velocity dispersion in $\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, $\langle I_r \rangle_e$ is the mean intensity inside the effective radius measured in $L_{\odot}$ pc$^{-2}$, and $\gamma$ is the distance-dependent zero point of the relation. Calibrating the zero point to the Leo I galaxy group, the constants in the FP relation become $\alpha = 1.24$, $\beta = 0.82$, and $\gamma = 2.194$.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: For NGC 4993 we measure $R_e = 15.5$ arcseconds, $\sigma = 171\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, and $\langle I_r \rangle_e = 407\,L_{\odot}$ pc$^{-2}$. Given that the scatter in the FP relation introduces an uncertainty in $D$ of $\pm 17\%$, calculate the distance to the galaxy (in Mpc) and its (absolute) uncertainty using the FP relation.
parts.statementAfter:
By measuring the amplitude (called strain, $h$) and the frequency of the gravitational waves, $f_{\mathrm{GW}}$, one can determine the distance to the source without having to rely on ‘standard candles’ like Cepheid variables or Type Ia supernovae. For two masses, $m_1$ and $m_2$, orbiting the centre of mass with separation $a$ with orbital angular velocity $\omega$, then the dimensionless strain parameter $h$ is

$$h \simeq \frac{G}{c^4} \frac{1}{r} \mu a^2 \omega^2$$

where $r$ is the luminosity distance, $c$ is the speed of light, $\mu = m_1 m_2 / M_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the reduced mass and $M_{\mathrm{tot}} = m_1 + m_2$ is the total mass.

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: Given that the gravitational frequency, $f_{\mathrm{GW}}$, is twice the orbital frequency (i.e. $f_{\mathrm{GW}} = \omega/\pi$) and the ‘chirp mass’, $\mathcal{M} = (\mu^3 M_{\mathrm{tot}}^2)^{1/5}$, express $h$ in terms of only $\mathcal{M}$, $r$, $f_{\mathrm{GW}}$, and various fundamental constants.
parts.statementAfter:
The rate of change of frequency of the gravitational waves (called the ‘chirp’) from a merging binary can be written as

$$\dot{f}_{\mathrm{GW}} = \frac{96}{5} \pi^{8/3} \left(\frac{G\mathcal{M}}{c^3}\right)^{5/3} f_{\mathrm{GW}}^{11/3}$$

parts.label: d.
parts.statement: Combine your result from c. with the above equation to cancel out $\mathcal{M}$ and so express the distance to the gravitational wave source, $r$, as a function of fundamental constants and the measurables $h$, $\dot{f}_{\mathrm{GW}}$, and $f_{\mathrm{GW}}$ only.

parts.label: e.
parts.statement: Typically, you measure $\tau \equiv f_{\mathrm{GW}}/\dot{f}_{\mathrm{GW}}$, rather than $\dot{f}_{\mathrm{GW}}$ directly. Given that just as the merger began the detectors measured $\tau = 0.0023$ s, $f_{\mathrm{GW}} = 300$ Hz and $h = 6.0 \times 10^{-21}$, estimate the distance to GW170817 (in Mpc) and its absolute uncertainty (assuming a percentage uncertainty of $\pm 10\%$). How does this compare with your answers in parts a. and b.?

answer.value: r = 41 ± 4 Mpc (41.3 Mpc), consistent with d and D within uncertainties

parts.label: f.
parts.statement: Using the redshift information from NGC 4993 and the gravitational wave distance you have just calculated, determine the Hubble constant $H_0$ in units of km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, along with its absolute uncertainty. Is this value consistent with the one derived by the HST using Cepheid variables (given in part a.)?

answer.value: H0 = 71 ± 13 km s^-1 Mpc^-1 (71.3), consistent with the HST value

solution.statement:
**Q2 - Multi-Messenger Astronomy** **[Total = 25]**

**a.**

$v = H_0 d \quad \therefore \quad d = \frac{v}{H_0} = \frac{cz}{H_0} = \frac{3.00 \times 10^{5} \times 0.00980}{73.24}$ (c must be in km s$^{-1}$) [1]

$= 40.1\ \mathrm{Mpc}$ [1]

Answer given to 3 s.f. as redshift has lowest precision (penalise more s.f.) [1] **[3]**

Uncertainty: $\frac{\Delta d}{d} = \frac{\Delta z}{z} + \frac{\Delta H_0}{H_0} = \frac{0.00079}{0.00980} + \frac{1.74}{73.24} (= 10.4\%)$ [1]

$\therefore \Delta d = 4.2\ \mathrm{Mpc}$ [1] **[2]**

Overall: $d = 40.1 \pm 4.2\ \mathrm{Mpc}$

[Allow uncertainties added in quadrature to give 8.4%, leading to Δd = 3.4 Mpc. Also, this is the only part of the question with a s.f. penalty]

**b.**

$D = \left(10^{-\log R_e + 1.24 \log \sigma - 0.82 \log \langle I_r \rangle_e + 2.194}\right)(1+z)^2$

$= \left(10^{-\log 15.5 + 1.24 \log 171 - 0.82 \log 407 + 2.194}\right)(1 + 0.00980)^2$ [1]

$= 43.8\ \mathrm{Mpc}$ [1] **[2]**

$\Delta D = 17\%$ of $43.8\ \mathrm{Mpc} = 7.4\ \mathrm{Mpc}$ [1] **[1]**

Overall: $D = 43.8 \pm 7.4\ \mathrm{Mpc}$

[Allow the uncertainty in z to be propagated too, giving ΔD = 14.5 Mpc or 9.0 Mpc (in quadrature)]

**c.**

Using Kepler's 3rd Law: $G M_{\mathrm{tot}} = a^3 \omega^2 \quad \therefore \quad a = \left(\frac{G M_{\mathrm{tot}}}{\omega^2}\right)^{1/3}$ [1]

Using the definition of chirp mass: $\mathcal{M} = (\mu^3 M_{\mathrm{tot}}^2)^{\frac{1}{5}} \quad \therefore \quad \mu = \left(\frac{\mathcal{M}^5}{M_{\mathrm{tot}}^2}\right)^{1/3}$ [1]

Putting these into the given equation: $h = \frac{G}{c^4} \frac{1}{r} \mu a^2 \omega^2$

$= \frac{G}{c^4} \frac{1}{r} \left(\frac{\mathcal{M}^5}{M_{\mathrm{tot}}^2}\right)^{1/3} \left(\frac{G M_{\mathrm{tot}}}{\omega^2}\right)^{2/3} \omega^2$ [1]

$= \frac{G^{5/3}}{c^4} \frac{1}{r} \mathcal{M}^{5/3} \omega^{2/3}$ [1]

Finally, using that $\omega = \pi f_{\mathrm{GW}}$: $\quad h = \frac{(G\mathcal{M})^{5/3}}{c^4} \frac{1}{r} \pi^{2/3} f_{\mathrm{GW}}^{2/3}$ [1] **[5]**

**d.**

Given that $\dot{f}_{\mathrm{GW}} = \frac{96}{5} \pi^{8/3} \left(\frac{G\mathcal{M}}{c^3}\right)^{5/3} f_{\mathrm{GW}}^{11/3} \quad \therefore \quad (G\mathcal{M})^{5/3} = \frac{5}{96} \frac{c^5 \dot{f}_{\mathrm{GW}}}{\pi^{8/3} f_{\mathrm{GW}}^{11/3}}$ [1]

Using our result from part c. $\quad (G\mathcal{M})^{5/3} = \frac{h r c^4}{\pi^{2/3} f_{\mathrm{GW}}^{2/3}}$ [1]

Combining these together: $\frac{5}{96} \frac{c^5 \dot{f}_{\mathrm{GW}}}{\pi^{8/3} f_{\mathrm{GW}}^{11/3}} = \frac{h r c^4}{\pi^{2/3} f_{\mathrm{GW}}^{2/3}} \quad \therefore \quad r = \frac{5}{96} \frac{c}{h\pi^2} \frac{\dot{f}_{\mathrm{GW}}}{f_{\mathrm{GW}}^3}$ [1] **[3]**

**e.**

$r = \frac{5}{96} \frac{c}{h\pi^2} \frac{1}{\tau f_{\mathrm{GW}}^2} = \frac{5}{96} \times \frac{3.00 \times 10^{8}}{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times \pi^2} \times \frac{1}{0.0023 \times 300}$ [1]

$= 1.27 \times 10^{24}\ \mathrm{m} = 41.3\ \mathrm{Mpc}$ [1] **[2]**

$\Delta r = 10\%$ of $41.3\ \mathrm{Mpc} = 4.1\ \mathrm{Mpc}$ [1] **[1]**

Overall: $r = 41 \pm 4\ \mathrm{Mpc}$

The values of d, D and r are consistent with each other within their uncertainties [1] **[1]**

**f.**

$v = H_0 r \quad \therefore \quad H_0 = \frac{v}{r} = \frac{cz}{r} = \frac{3.00 \times 10^{5} \times 0.00980}{41.3}$ (c must be in km s$^{-1}$) [1]

$= 71.3\ \mathrm{km\ s^{-1}\ Mpc^{-1}}$ [1] **[2]**

Uncertainty: $\frac{\Delta H_0}{H_0} = \frac{\Delta z}{z} + \frac{\Delta r}{r} = \frac{0.00079}{0.00980} + 0.1 \quad (= 18.1\%)$ [1]

$\therefore \Delta H_0 = 12.9\ \mathrm{km\ s^{-1}\ Mpc^{-1}}$ [1] **[2]**

Overall: $H_0 = 71 \pm 13\ \mathrm{km\ s^{-1}\ Mpc^{-1}}$

The value of H$_0$ derived from multi-messenger astronomy **is consistent** with the value derived by the HST using Cepheid variables [1] **[1]**

[Allow uncertainties added in quadrature, giving ΔH$_0$ = 9.2 km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$]

problems.title: Great American Eclipse
problems.statement:
On 21st August 2017 the continental United States experienced a total solar eclipse. Dubbed the ‘Great American Eclipse’, it was estimated to be one of the most watched eclipses in history.

The path of totality (where the Moon completely obscures the Sun) is shown in Figure 3, and the point of greatest eclipse (“GE”; where the path was widest since the axis of the cone of the Moon’s shadow passed closest to the centre of the Earth) was near the village of Cerulean, Kentucky. The following data can be used for this question:

- The angular radii of the Sun and the Moon (if observed from the centre of the Earth) at the moment of GE are $15'48.7''$ and $16'03.4''$, respectively, where the notation $xx'yy.y''$ corresponds to $xx$ arcminutes and $yy.y$ arcseconds (60 arcminutes = 1 degree, and 60 arcseconds = 1 arcminute)
- The latitude and longitude of the location of GE are $36^{\circ}58.0'$N and $87^{\circ}40.3'$W, respectively
- Take the mean radii of the Sun, Earth and Moon to be respectively $R_{\odot} = 695\,700$ km, $R_{\oplus} = 6371$ km and $R_{\mathrm{Moon}} = 1737$ km, and a day to be 24 hours
- Take the semi-major axes of the Sun-Earth and Earth-Moon systems to be $149\,600\,000$ km and $384\,400$ km, respectively
- As viewed from a location far above the North Pole, the Moon orbits in an anticlockwise direction around the Earth, and the Earth spins in an anticlockwise direction

For an ellipse with semi-major axis $a$ it can be shown that the velocity $v$, at a distance $r$ from mass $M$, can be written as:

$$v^2 = GM\left(\frac{2}{r} - \frac{1}{a}\right)$$

figures.caption: Figure 3: The path of totality for the Great American Eclipse. The narrow dimension is its width. Credit: Fred Espenak, NASA’s GSFC.
figures.alt: Globe map titled “Total Solar Eclipse of 2017 Aug 21” centred on North America, with compass marks N, E, S, W. A narrow blue band (path of totality) crosses the United States from the north-west to the south-east; an arrow marks “Greatest Eclipse” in the middle of the USA. Green lines are labelled with times 17:00 UT to 20:00 UT, blue curves with eclipse magnitudes 0.20, 0.40, 0.60, 0.80; pink limit curves are marked P1–P4, and an arrow marks the “Sub Solar” point.

figures.caption: Figure 4: The route of the Moon’s shadow in the vicinity of the points of greatest duration (GD, near Carbondale) and greatest eclipse (GE, near Hopkinsville). Any places between the two limits on the path of totality will experience at least a very short period of totality - outside that region will only be a partial eclipse - and the perpendicular distance between them is the path width. The longest duration of totality at that point of the shadow’s journey is indicated as the path of maximum totality, which both GE and GD sit on. The closest part of that path to Carbondale is indicated as CP. Credit: Fred Espenak & Google Maps.
figures.alt: Road map of southern Illinois, western Kentucky and surroundings (towns such as Carbondale, Marion, Cape Girardeau, Paducah, Evansville, Hopkinsville, Clarksville). Two parallel purple lines labelled “Path of totality limits” run from upper left to lower right; a red line between them is labelled “Path of maximum totality”. A purple pin “GD” lies on the red line near Carbondale, a black dot “CP” marks the closest point to Carbondale, and a green pin “GE” lies on the red line near Hopkinsville.

Diagram of an elliptical orbit (from the constants page): ellipse with dashed major axis from P (left) through focus F (blue dot) and centre O to A (right), labelled a between O and A; dashed minor axis from B (top) to C (bottom), labelled b between O and B.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Calculate the width of the path of totality at GE (in km). You may use the approximation that the Moon is directly overhead so that the shadow is circular, and small enough that the curvature of the Earth can be neglected.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: Show that at this point the shadow is moving across the Earth’s surface at approximately $0.68\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. You may use the simplifying approximation that for short time intervals it can be considered as travelling with a constant latitude, and that the apparent movement of the Sun due to the Earth’s orbit can be neglected.

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: Hence calculate the duration of the eclipse. Give your answer to the nearest 0.1 s.
parts.statementAfter: The point of greatest eclipse and greatest duration do not generally coincide, as a more elliptical shadow with a major axis aligned with the path of maximum totality (and thinner path width, equal to the minor axis) can compensate for the shadow moving faster at higher latitudes. For this eclipse the point of greatest duration (“GD”) was at co-ordinates of $37^{\circ}35'$N latitude and $89^{\circ}07'$W longitude, reached about 4 minutes before GE, and where totality lasted 0.1 s longer than the value calculated in part c.

parts.label: d. (i)
parts.statement:
d. The town of Carbondale, Illinois, is the closest big town to the point of GD, with co-ordinates $37^{\circ}44'$N latitude and $89^{\circ}13'$W longitude. Assuming the path of maximum totality can be treated as linear as it passes through the region around GD and GE:

(i) Calculate the co-ordinates of the closest point (“CP”) to Carbondale on the path of maximum totality.

parts.label: d. (ii)
parts.statement: Calculate the distance (in km) between Carbondale and CP.

parts.label: d. (iii)
parts.statement: Hence calculate (to the nearest 0.1 s) how much shorter totality was for residents in Carbondale compared with CP. Take the duration at CP to be the same as GD, the width of the path to be 0.5 km less than for GE (so the Moon’s shadow is elliptical), and the speed of the Moon’s shadow to have only been affected by the change in latitude.

solution.statement:
**Q3 - Great American Eclipse** **[Total = 25]**

**a.**

Suitable diagram [1]

From the apparent angular radii we can calculate the distance to the Moon and the Sun:

Moon: $16'03.4'' = 4.67 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{rad} \quad \therefore d_{\mathrm{Moon}} = \frac{R_{\mathrm{Moon}}}{\theta} = \frac{1737}{4.67 \times 10^{-3}} = 371\,900\ \mathrm{km}$ [1]

Sun: $15'48.7'' = 4.60 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{rad} \quad \therefore d_{\mathrm{Sun}} = \frac{R_{\mathrm{Sun}}}{\theta} = \frac{695700}{4.60 \times 10^{-3}} = 151\,258\,000\ \mathrm{km}$ [1]

Angle of shadow: $\alpha = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{R_{\mathrm{Sun}} - R_{\mathrm{Moon}}}{d_{\mathrm{Sun}} - d_{\mathrm{Moon}}}\right) = 4.60 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{rad} \quad (= 0.2635^{\circ})$ [1]

Shadow cone length: $d_{\mathrm{umbra}} = \frac{R_{\mathrm{Moon}}}{\sin\alpha} = 377\,670\ \mathrm{km}$ [1]

Full width of shadow: $s_{\mathrm{umbra}} = 2\left(d_{\mathrm{umbra}} - (d_{\mathrm{Moon}} - R_{\mathrm{Earth}})\right)\tan\alpha = 111.7\ \mathrm{km}$ [1] **[6]**

[Allow s$_{\mathrm{umbra}}$ = 55.9 km if it is clear that the student recognises that's the radius of the circular shadow, otherwise they lose one mark. Allow use of small angle approximations throughout or other slight variations in the geometry resulting in a width within a few km of the correct answer]

**b.**

At GE, the latitude is $\theta = 36^{\circ}58' = 36.967^{\circ}$

$v_{\mathrm{rot}} = \frac{2\pi R_E \cos\theta}{T} = \frac{2\pi \times 6371 \times \cos 36.967}{24 \times 60 \times 60}$ [1]

$= 0.370\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ [1]

$v^2 = GM\left(\frac{2}{r} - \frac{1}{a}\right) \quad \therefore v_{\mathrm{Moon}} = \sqrt{GM_E\left(\frac{2}{d_{\mathrm{Moon}}} - \frac{1}{a}\right)}$

$= \sqrt{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 5.97 \times 10^{24}\left(\frac{2}{371900 \times 10^{3}} - \frac{1}{384400 \times 10^{3}}\right)}$ [1]

$= 1.051\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ [1]

Hence: $v_{\mathrm{rel}} = v_{\mathrm{Moon}} - v_{\mathrm{rot}} = 1.051 - 0.370 = 0.681\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ [1] **[5]**

[Since this is a 'show that' question, ensure the student has shown evidence that they have calculated the correct relative velocity (rather than simply quoted it) for the final mark]

**c.**

$t_{\mathrm{eclipse}} = \frac{s_{\mathrm{umbra}}}{v_{\mathrm{rel}}} = \frac{111.74}{0.681} = 164.0\ \mathrm{s} \quad (= 2\ \mathrm{mins}\ 44.0\ \mathrm{secs})$ [1] **[1]**

[Answer must be to the nearest 0.1 s for the mark]

Despite many of the simplifying assumptions made, this is within a few seconds of the measured value of 2 mins 41.6 secs or the official predicted value of 2 mins 40.3 secs

**d. (i)**

Converting the co-ordinates of GE and GD:

GE: $x_1 = 87.67^{\circ}, y_1 = 36.97^{\circ}$ $\quad$ GD: $x_2 = 89.12^{\circ}, y_2 = 37.58^{\circ}$

Equation of a straight line is $y = mx + c$, so:

$m = \frac{x_2 - x_1}{y_2 - y_1} = 0.427$ [1]

$c = y_1 - m x_1 = -0.448$ [1]

[Allow reversed signs of m and c so long as internally consistent]

Equation of the line passing through Cardondale (with co-ordinates x$_{\mathrm{C}}$, y$_{\mathrm{C}}$) and perpendicular to the initial line at CP (with co-ordinates x$_{\mathrm{CP}}$, y$_{\mathrm{CP}}$) must satisfy

$m x_{CP} + c = -\frac{1}{m}(x_{CP} - x_C) + y_C$ [1]

$\therefore x_{CP} = \frac{x_C + m y_C - mc}{m^2 + 1} = 89.26^{\circ} \quad (= 89^{\circ}15.3')$ [1]

$y_{CP} = m x_{CP} + c = 37.64^{\circ} \quad (= 37^{\circ}38.6')$ [1] **[5]**

**d. (ii)**

We can calculate the angular distance, utilising Pythagoras' theorem since they are very close together:

$\theta_{\mathrm{dist}} = \sqrt{(x_{CP} - x_C)^2 + (y_{CP} - y_C)^2} = 0.0987^{\circ} = 0.0017\ \mathrm{rad}$ [1]

Using the small angle approximation (and ignoring the surface curvature on this scale):

$d = \theta_{\mathrm{dist}} \times R_E = 0.0017 \times 6371 = 11.0\ \mathrm{km}$ [1] **[2]**

**d. (iii)**

At CP: $t_{\mathrm{eclipse,CP}} = 164.1\ \mathrm{s} \quad s_{\mathrm{umbra,CP}} = s_{\mathrm{umbra}} - 0.5 = 111.24\ \mathrm{km}$

$v_{\mathrm{Moon}} = 1.051\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ (same as before)

$v_{\mathrm{rot,CP}} = \frac{2\pi R_E \cos(y_{CP})}{T} = 0.367\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}} \quad \therefore v_{\mathrm{rel,CP}} = 0.684\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ [1]

Eclipse shadow is now elliptical with:

Minor axis $= s_{\mathrm{umbra,CP}} = 111.24\ \mathrm{km}$

Major axis $= t_{\mathrm{eclipse,CP}} \times v_{\mathrm{rel,CP}} = 112.36\ \mathrm{km}$ [1]

For an ellipse, $x = a\cos\theta$ and $y = b\sin\theta$

Hence if $y = 11.0\ \mathrm{km}$ and $b = \frac{111.24}{2} \quad \Rightarrow \theta = 11.38^{\circ} \quad \therefore x = 55.07\ \mathrm{km}$ [2]

[First mark is for an appropriate diagram and use of the equation of an ellipse]

So the length of the shadow over Carbondale $= 2x = 110.1\ \mathrm{km}$ [1]

$\therefore t_{\mathrm{eclipse,C}} = \frac{110.1}{0.684} = 160.9\ \mathrm{s}$

$\therefore \Delta t = 164.1 - 160.9 = 3.2\ \mathrm{s}$ [1] **[6]**

[Answer must be to the nearest 0.1 s for the mark]

Carbondale is lucky enough that it will also be on the path of totality of the next eclipse to cross the mainland of the USA on 8th April 2024!

figures.alt: Geometry of the umbra: a large circle (Sun) with radius R_Sun on the left, a small circle (Moon) with radius R_M and a medium circle (Earth) with radius R_E on the right. Two tangent lines from the Sun’s limbs past the Moon converge to a point beyond the Earth, making angle α with the axis; the red segment s_umbra marks the shadow width at the Earth. Distances d_Sun (Sun to Earth centre), d_Moon (Moon to Earth centre) and d_umbra (Moon to cone apex) are marked with arrows.

Ellipse with dashed horizontal and vertical axes through the centre; semi-axes labelled a (horizontal) and b (vertical); a radius line drawn at angle θ to the horizontal axis meets the ellipse at a point whose projections are labelled x (on the horizontal axis) and y (on the vertical axis).

problems.title: Super-Earths and Planet Nine
problems.statement:
Recent years have seen an explosion in the discovery of new exoplanets. About 85% of transiting exoplanets discovered by the NASA Kepler telescope have radii less than Neptune ($\sim 4\,R_{\oplus}$), meaning we are improving our understanding of what the transition between rocky Earth-size planets and gaseous Neptune-size planets looks like.

Given how common these “super-Earths” and “gas dwarfs” seem to be, it was odd that we didn’t have any in our own Solar System. However, Batygin & Brown (2016) suggested that a hypothetical ninth planet (called ‘Planet Nine’) could explain some of the unusual properties of the orbits of objects in the Kuiper Belt. This planet is inferred to have a mass of $10\,M_{\oplus}$, and so would be an example of a super-Earth.

Analysing exoplanets discovered by Kepler, Marcy *et al.* (2014) used a piecewise function to describe their planetary density data such that:

| | |
|---|---|
| For $R_{\mathrm{P}} \le 1.5\,R_{\oplus}$ | $\rho = 2.32 + 3.18\frac{R_{\mathrm{P}}}{R_{\oplus}}$ [g cm$^{-3}$] |
| For $1.5\,R_{\oplus} < R_{\mathrm{P}} \le 4.2\,R_{\oplus}$ | $\frac{M_{\mathrm{P}}}{M_{\oplus}} = 2.69\left(\frac{R_{\mathrm{P}}}{R_{\oplus}}\right)^{0.93}$ |

where $R_{\mathrm{P}}$ is the radius of the planet, $M_{\mathrm{P}}$ is the mass of the planet, and the model’s transition between rocky super-Earth and non-rocky gas dwarf occurs at $R_{\mathrm{P}} = 1.5\,R_{\oplus}$.

figures.caption: Figure 5: A plot of planet density versus radius for 33 extrasolar planets (circles) and the planets in our solar system (diamonds). Credit: Marcy et al. (2014).
figures.alt: Scatter plot of “Planet Density [g cm^-3]” (0 to 15) against “Planet Radius [R_Earth]” (about 0.5 to 4.2). Points with error bars; a dashed straight line labelled “ρ=2.32 + 3.18 R/R_E” rises up to about 1.5 R_Earth, then a solid curve labelled “(M/M_E) = 2.69 * (R/R_E)^0.93” falls with radius. Diamonds mark solar-system planets.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Based on the Marcy *et al.* (2014) model, Planet Nine is most likely to be a gas dwarf with a thick gaseous envelope. Calculate $R_{\mathrm{P}}$ (in units of $R_{\oplus}$) for Planet Nine using this model.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: Planetary formation models suggest such a gas dwarf would have a solid rocky core the size of the Earth, with similar composition and density. Calculate a simple estimate of the atmospheric pressure on the rocky surface. Compare your answer to the atmospheric pressure at sea level on the Earth, $p_{\oplus} = 100$ kPa.

answer.note: About a million times larger than atmospheric pressure on Earth.

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: In practice the transition between rocky and gaseous planets is not likely to be sharply at 1.5 $R_{\oplus}$, with some planets of both types existing above and below the limit. Calculate $R_{\mathrm{P}}$ (in units of $R_{\oplus}$) for Planet Nine if it was a rocky super-Earth. How does its average density compare to an Earth-sized rocky exoplanet?
parts.statementAfter:
The minimum speed necessary to fully escape a planet’s gravity (rather than be put into an elliptical orbit) is called the escape velocity and is calculated as

$$v_{\mathrm{esc}} = \sqrt{\frac{2GM_{\mathrm{P}}}{R_{\mathrm{P}}}}$$

where $G$ is the universal gravitational constant.

In contrast, the maximum speed a rocket can provide is determined by the ejection velocity, $v_{\mathrm{e}}$, of the gas used, as determined by the chemical energy stored in the bonds of the fuel used, and the fraction of the rocket that is fuel. Since the rocket gets lighter as it burns its fuel the final speed can be bigger than $v_{\mathrm{e}}$. The rocket equation is

$$v_{\mathrm{max}} = v_{\mathrm{e}} \ln\frac{m_0}{m_1}$$

where $m_0$ is the mass at launch and $m_1$ is the mass once all the fuel has been burnt. The most energetic chemical reaction we can use in a rocket is hydrogen-oxygen, which gives $v_{\mathrm{e}} = 4.46\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, and engineering limits us to a rocket design with a maximum of 96% of launch mass being fuel (as was used with the solid rockets that launched the space shuttle).

parts.label: d.
parts.statement: Verify that the above rocket design is sufficient to escape from Earth but **not** sufficient to escape from the surface of a rocky Planet Nine.

answer.value: v_max = 14.4 km/s; v_esc,Earth = 11.2 km/s < v_max < v_esc,PN = 25.8 km/s

parts.label: e.
parts.statement: Calculate the maximum value of $R_{\mathrm{P}}$ (for a rocky exoplanet) above which any alien civilization would be unable to escape their planet’s gravity using simple chemical rocket propulsion systems. (They could of course still have orbital satellites, since the speeds for planetary orbit are lower.)

parts.label: f.
parts.statement: In the Marcy *et al.* (2014) model, above $R_{\mathrm{P}} = 1.5\,R_{\oplus}$ the density of gas dwarfs rapidly decreases with radius. By looking at the piecewise function explain why this does **not** improve the situation for any alien civilization living on such a gas dwarf hoping to explore their solar system. You do not need to calculate any new escape velocities.

answer.value: For gas dwarfs M_P ∝ R_P^0.93 ≈ R_P, so v_esc ~ constant, about the value for a rocky planet with R_P = 1.5 R⊕ > 1.21 R⊕; the rocket is insufficient for all gas dwarfs.

solution.statement:
**Q4 - Super-Earths and Planet Nine** **[Total = 25]**

**a.**

$\frac{R_P}{R_E} = \left(\frac{M_P/M_E}{2.69}\right)^{1/0.93} = \left(\frac{10}{2.69}\right)^{1/0.93}$ [1]

$= 4.10\ R_E$ [1] **[2]**

[Allow 1 mark max if they forget to raise to the power of 1/0.93, giving R$_{\mathrm{P}}$ = 3.72 R$_{\mathrm{E}}$]

**b.**

$V_{\mathrm{atm}} = V_{\mathrm{planet}} - V_{\mathrm{core}} = \frac{4}{3}\pi(4.10\ R_E)^3 - \frac{4}{3}\pi R_E^3$

$= \frac{4}{3}\pi(4.10^3 - 1^3)(6.37 \times 10^{6})^3 = 7.37 \times 10^{22}\ \mathrm{m}$ [1]

$M_{\mathrm{atm}} = M_{\mathrm{planet}} - M_{\mathrm{core}} = 9\ M_E \quad (= 5.37 \times 10^{25}\ \mathrm{kg})$ [1]

$\rho_{\mathrm{atm}} = \frac{M_{\mathrm{atm}}}{V_{\mathrm{atm}}} = \frac{5.37 \times 10^{25}}{7.37 \times 10^{22}} = 729\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}} \quad (= 0.73\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}})$ [1]

$p_{\mathrm{atm}} = \rho_{\mathrm{atm}} \times g \times h_{\mathrm{atm}} = 729 \times 9.81 \times (4.10 - 1) R_E$

$= 1.41 \times 10^{11}\ \mathrm{Pa}$ [1] **[4]**

This is about a million times larger than atmospheric pressure on Earth [1] **[1]**

[Allow other models for atmospheric pressure, such as taking the weight of the whole atmosphere and applying it to the surface area of an Earth-sized core, giving 1.03 × 10$^{12}$ Pa. Don't expect to see any attempt to model the variation in *g* or ρ with height since it only asked for a simple estimate]

**c.**

$\rho = 1000\left[2.32 + 3.18\left(\frac{R_P}{R_E}\right)\right] = \frac{M_P}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_P^3}$

$\therefore \frac{3180}{R_E} R_P^4 + 2320 R_P^3 - \frac{M_P}{\frac{4}{3}\pi} = 0$ [1]

Only positive real root is $R_P = 1.20 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m} = 1.88\ R_E$ [3] **[4]**

$\rho_{\mathrm{Earth}} = 2.32 + 3.18 = 5.50\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ [1]

$\rho_{\mathrm{av}} = 2.32 + (3.18 \times 1.88) = 8.30\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}} = 1.51\ \rho_{\mathrm{Earth}}$ [1] **[2]**

[Allow any valid method to solve the quartic, such as using their graphical calculator to plot the graph and find roots, or even a trial and error iteration. If when constructing the quartic they forget to convert the densities into kg m$^{-3}$ (leading to R$_{\mathrm{P}}$ = 7.20 × 10$^{7}$ m = 11.3 R$_{\mathrm{E}}$) then only lose 1 mark]

**d.**

$v_{\mathrm{max}} = v_{\mathrm{e}} \ln\frac{m_0}{m_1} = 4.46 \ln\left(\frac{1}{1 - 0.96}\right) = 14.4\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ [1]

$v_{\mathrm{esc,Earth}} = \sqrt{\frac{2GM_E}{R_E}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 6.67 \times 10^{11} \times 5.97 \times 10^{24}}{6.37 \times 10^{6}}} = 11.2\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ [1]

$v_{\mathrm{esc,PN}} = \sqrt{\frac{2GM_P}{R_P}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 6.67 \times 10^{11} \times (10 \times 5.97 \times 10^{24})}{(1.88 \times 6.37 \times 10^{6})}} = 25.8\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ [1] **[3]**

$v_{\mathrm{esc,Earth}} < v_{\mathrm{max}} < v_{\mathrm{esc,PN}}$ [1] **[1]**

So this rocket design is able to allow us to escape Earth's gravity, but is far short of what is needed for Planet Nine (which has implications for any probe that ever lands on it, should it exist)

[Allow the comparisons to be done in terms of gravitational potential rather than escape velocities. If the student **did not** get a value of R$_{\mathrm{P}}$ in part c. then allow them to use their value of R$_{\mathrm{P}}$ from part a. for full credit (giving v$_{\mathrm{esc,PN}}$ = 17.5 km s$^{-1}$ for R$_{\mathrm{P}}$ = 4.10 R$_{\mathrm{E}}$)]

**e.**

$M_P = 1000\left[2.32 + 3.18\left(\frac{R_{P,\mathrm{max}}}{R_E}\right)\right] \times \frac{4}{3}\pi R_{P,\mathrm{max}}^3$

$v_{\mathrm{max}}^2 = \frac{2GM_P}{R_{P,\mathrm{max}}} = \frac{2G}{R_{P,\mathrm{max}}} \times 1000\left[2.32 + 3.18\left(\frac{R_{P,\mathrm{max}}}{R_E}\right)\right] \times \frac{4}{3}\pi R_{P,\mathrm{max}}^3$ [1]

$\therefore \frac{3180}{R_E} R_{P,\mathrm{max}}^3 + 2320 R_{P,\mathrm{max}}^2 - \frac{v_{\mathrm{max}}^2}{\frac{8}{3}\pi G} = 0$ [1]

Only positive real root is $R_{P,\mathrm{max}} = 7.73 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{m} \quad (= 1.21\ R_E)$ [3] **[5]**

[Allow any valid method to solve the cubic, such as using their graphical calculator to plot the graph and find roots, or even a trial and error iteration. If when constructing the cubic they forget to convert the densities into kg m$^{-3}$ (leading to R$_{\mathrm{P,max}}$ = 8.89 × 10$^{7}$ m = 14.0 R$_{\mathrm{E}}$) then only lose 1 mark. Forgetting to express v$_{\mathrm{max}}$ in m s$^{-1}$ leads to nonsensical values of R$_{\mathrm{P,max}}$ (less than R$_{\mathrm{E}}$) given they should only be looking at the positive roots]

**f.**

In the model for gas dwarfs $M_P \propto R_P^{0.93} \approx M_P \propto R_P$ [1]

Since $v_{\mathrm{esc}} \propto \sqrt{\frac{M_P}{R_P}}$ then if $M_P \propto R_P \Rightarrow v_{\mathrm{esc}} \sim \mathrm{constant}$ [1]

(So the escape velocity will be roughly the same for all gas dwarfs, and approximately the same as the escape velocity for a rocky planet with R$_{\mathrm{P}}$ = 1.5 R$_{\mathrm{E}}$)

Rocket design gives insufficient thrust at R$_{\mathrm{P}}$ > 1.21 R$_{\mathrm{E}}$, so will be insufficient at 1.5 R$_{\mathrm{E}}$, and hence will be insufficient for all gas dwarfs too [1] **[3]**

END OF PAPER
